title: Sets, queues, stacks and priority queues
body: `HashSet<T>` stores unique elements with O(1) average `Add`, `Remove` and `Contains`; `Add` returns false for a duplicate. Set operations (`UnionWith`, `IntersectWith`, `ExceptWith`, `IsSubsetOf`) modify the set in place. `SortedSet<T>` keeps elements ordered at O(log n) per operation.

`Queue<T>` is first-in first-out: `Enqueue`, `Dequeue`, `Peek`. `Stack<T>` is last-in first-out: `Push`, `Pop`, `Peek`. Both throw `InvalidOperationException` when empty; `TryDequeue` and `TryPop` avoid that. A queue drives breadth-first search; a stack drives depth-first search and undo histories.

`PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority>` dequeues the element with the smallest priority first (a min-heap). Enqueue and dequeue are O(log n). Elements with equal priority come out in no guaranteed order, so add a tie-breaker to the priority (for example a tuple of priority and sequence number) when stability matters.
`LinkedList<T>` offers O(1) insertion and removal at a known node but poor cache behaviour; it is rarely the fastest choice in practice. Measure before reaching for it.
Check empty-collection behaviour before every Dequeue, Pop or Peek, and check whether ties in a priority queue need a deterministic order.

challenge: Use a Queue to do a breadth-first search on the graph a->[b,c], b->[d], c->[d,e], d->[], e->[] starting at a, printing nodes in visit order without repeats.
question: Which item does PriorityQueue<TElement, int> dequeue first?
correct: The element with the smallest priority value
wrong: The element with the largest priority value
reasoning: It is a min-heap; ties are not ordered, so add a sequence number to the priority for stability.
